clinicalPearls: A clonal proliferative disorder of Langerhans-type dendritic cells that can range from a single isolated lesion to widespread multisystem disease.
Bone is the most commonly involved site, often presenting as a painful lytic lesion, classically in the skull but also in other flat and long bones.
Skin involvement can mimic seborrhoeic dermatitis or a persistent scaly, petechial rash, particularly in infants.
Diabetes insipidus from pituitary or hypothalamic involvement is a characteristic endocrine manifestation and may be the presenting feature.
Risk organ involvement (liver, spleen, and bone marrow) identifies higher-risk multisystem disease with greater mortality.
Diagnosis rests on biopsy showing characteristic cells expressing CD1a and CD207 (langerin); Birbeck granules may be seen on electron microscopy.
Many cases harbour activating mutations in the MAPK pathway, most commonly BRAF V600E, which has therapeutic implications.
Treatment ranges from observation or local therapy for single-system disease to systemic chemotherapy for multisystem or risk-organ disease.
reference.pathophysiology: Langerhans cell histiocytosis is now understood as a myeloid neoplasm driven by activating mutations of the MAPK/ERK signalling pathway, most often BRAF V600E, in dendritic cell precursors. Constitutive pathway activation causes accumulation of pathological CD1a-positive, langerin-positive histiocytes that, together with eosinophils and other inflammatory cells, form granulomatous infiltrates. These lesions destroy local tissue (such as lytic bone lesions) and, when disseminated, impair function of organs including the liver, spleen, marrow, and pituitary.
additionalDifferentials: Osteomyelitis or Ewing sarcoma (for bone lesions)
Seborrhoeic or atopic dermatitis (for skin lesions)
Other histiocytic disorders (e.g. haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis, juvenile xanthogranuloma)
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy with immunohistochemistry for CD1a and CD207 (langerin)
BRAF V600E and broader MAPK pathway mutation testing
Skeletal imaging survey (radiographs and/or PET) to map bone lesions
Assessment of risk organs: liver and spleen imaging, full blood count, liver function
Endocrine evaluation and MRI of the pituitary/hypothalamus if diabetes insipidus is suspected
Baseline evaluation for pulmonary and CNS involvement when indicated
redFlags: Risk-organ (liver, spleen, marrow) involvement indicating high-risk multisystem disease
Polyuria and polydipsia indicating diabetes insipidus from CNS/pituitary disease
Rapidly progressive multisystem disease in an infant
Neurodegenerative CNS involvement causing progressive neurological decline
reference.prognosis: Single-system disease, especially isolated bone lesions, often has an excellent prognosis and may even regress; multisystem disease with risk-organ involvement carries higher mortality. Survivors are at risk of long-term sequelae such as diabetes insipidus, other endocrinopathies, orthopaedic problems, and neurodegeneration.
pitfalls: Mistaking the infantile skin rash for simple seborrhoeic dermatitis and delaying diagnosis
Overlooking diabetes insipidus as an early or isolated manifestation
Assuming a solitary lytic bone lesion is infection or a benign cyst without biopsy
Failing to assess for risk-organ involvement, which changes treatment intensity and prognosis
management: Treat isolated single-system bone lesions with local measures such as observation, curettage or intralesional corticosteroid
Treat multisystem or multifocal disease with systemic chemotherapy, standardly vinblastine combined with a corticosteroid such as prednisolone
Use targeted MAPK-pathway inhibitors - BRAF inhibitors such as vemurafenib or dabrafenib, or MEK inhibitors - for BRAF V600E-mutated or refractory disease
Manage endocrine sequelae, notably desmopressin for diabetes insipidus and replacement of other deficient pituitary hormones
Assess and monitor risk organs (liver, spleen and bone marrow) to identify high-risk disease and guide salvage therapy
Provide long-term surveillance for late sequelae including endocrinopathy, neurodegenerative CNS involvement and pulmonary disease, with smoking cessation for pulmonary disease
Coordinate multidisciplinary care through paediatric haematology-oncology and endocrinology, escalating to salvage regimens for risk-organ or refractory disease
